content_units: 90-Minute Jazz Path at a Glance

A melody-first route from big-band swing to modal jazz and electric fusion, tuned for an indie-rock listener. To keep it near   90 minutes   while using   exactly 8 albums  , this path works best as a   guided sampler  : listen to   1 standout track per album in order  , plus the short cues below.
8-Album Evolution Route
Album   Era/Style   Standout Track   What to listen for   Approx. track time

1   Duke Ellington —  Ellington at Newport    Swing / big band     Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue     Call-and-response riffs, section interplay, the excitement of repetition building like a live indie jam   14 min

2   Lester Young —  The President Plays with the Oscar Peterson Trio    Late swing / cool-leaning small group     Ad Lib Blues     Relaxed phrasing, conversational soloing, how jazz can feel intimate instead of orchestral   7 min

3   Miles Davis —  'Round About Midnight    Bebop into lyric hard bop     'Round Midnight     Mood, space, and melody-first improvisation; notice how the tune stays central even as solos branch out   6 min

4   Art Blakey & the Jazz Messengers —  Moanin’    Hard bop / gospel-blues feel     Moanin’     Big hook, earthy piano intro, punchy horns; this is one of the easiest bridges from rock songwriting to jazz structure   10 min

5   Dave Brubeck Quartet —  Time Out    Cool jazz / rhythmic experiment     Blue Rondo à la Turk     Unusual meter used in a catchy way; focus on how odd time can still feel propulsive and memorable   7 min
6   John Coltrane —  My Favorite Things    Modal jazz     My Favorite Things     Repetition over fewer chords, trance-like momentum, and how a familiar melody becomes a long-form exploration   13 min
7   Miles Davis —  Kind of Blue    Modal jazz     So What     Spacious harmony, less chord-chasing, more mood and shape; hear how simplicity opens the door to deeper groove   9 min

8   Herbie Hancock —  Head Hunters    Jazz fusion / funk     Chameleon     Electric bassline, layered groove, studio texture; the clearest landing point if you like rhythm-forward modern bands   15 min
Total listening for the standout tracks:   about 81 minutes  .

Use the remaining    9 minutes   to replay your favorite two tracks or add the opening of  Take Five  from  Time Out  and  Cantaloupe Island  from Hancock’s earlier work if you want a little extra context.
What Changes from Album to Album
1) From swing to small-group intimacy
Start with   Ellington  , where jazz is arranged, dramatic, and communal.
By   Lester Young  , the music feels looser and more personal, like the room got smaller and the conversation sharper.
2) From melody to improvisational personality
With   Miles Davis   on  'Round About Midnight  and   Blakey   on  Moanin’ , the tunes are still memorable, but the solos begin to matter as much as the written themes.
This is where jazz starts to feel like songwriting plus real-time reinvention.
3) From chord movement to modal space
Brubeck   stretches rhythm;   Coltrane   and   Kind of Blue   stretch harmony.
Instead of lots of chord changes, modal jazz lets players sit inside a mood longer, which often makes it easier for new listeners to lock into the feel.
4) From acoustic swing to electric groove
Head Hunters   keeps the jazz instinct for improvisation but delivers it through funk repetition, keyboards, and bass-driven momentum.
If indie rock often hooks you with texture and groove, this is the most direct crossover point.
Album-by-Album Listening Notes
1. Duke Ellington —  Ellington at Newport
- Best first step because it’s vivid, live, and full of big melodic gestures.
- Listen for how riffs repeat and intensify rather than just “show off” technique.
-   Standout track:    Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue
2. Lester Young —  The President Plays with the Oscar Peterson Trio
- A softer landing after big-band swing.
- Young’s tone is light and lyrical; it often feels closer to singing than to virtuoso display.
-   Standout track:    Ad Lib Blues
3. Miles Davis —  'Round About Midnight
- Think of this as late-night cinematic jazz with a strong emotional center.
- Notice how restraint creates tension; not every solo is dense.
-   Standout track:    'Round Midnight
4. Art Blakey & the Jazz Messengers —  Moanin’
- Probably the most instantly catchy album here.
- Gospel, blues, and hard-driving rhythm make it especially friendly for rock listeners.
-   Standout track:    Moanin’
5. Dave Brubeck Quartet —  Time Out
- Shows that jazz experimentation can still be tuneful.
- Focus on rhythm as the hook, not just the melody.
-   Standout track:    Blue Rondo à la Turk
6. John Coltrane —  My Favorite Things
- A great entry into Coltrane because the source melody is familiar and clear.
- Listen to how repetition becomes hypnotic rather than static.
-   Standout track:    My Favorite Things
7. Miles Davis —  Kind of Blue
- The classic modal reference point, but also one of the most melodic jazz records ever made.
- Hear how each solo feels spacious, almost architectural.
-   Standout track:    So What
8. Herbie Hancock —  Head Hunters
- Ends the path with groove, electronics, and a more modern pulse.
- You can hear how jazz evolves without abandoning memorable motifs.
-   Standout track:    Chameleon
